title: MB7-26178
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): This is an appeal made by XXXX XXXX XXXX against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on November 27, 2017, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: This is an appeal made by XXXX XXXX XXXX against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on November 27, 2017, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The appellant alleges a fear of returning to the Democratic Republic of Congo because as a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, he states that he was unjustly blamed for diverting funds earmarked for XXXX XXXX and was being forced to repay US XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Fearing that he would be imprisoned, tortured or possibly killed, he travelled to Kinshasa and then left the Congo on XXXX XXXX, 2016.

The Minister's representative intervened at the hearing before the RPD. He stated that the appellant's identity was not established as set out in paragraph 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),1 and therefore his claim for refugee protection should be rejected.
The RPD rejected the appellant's claim for refugee protection because he failed to establish his identity with reliable documents and because his explanations were not credible.

The appellant is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to [translation] "set aside the Immigration Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) determination; substitute its determination for the one made on November 27, 2017, or refer the matter to the Board...for redetermination."
The appellant is not requesting to present new evidence pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and does not want a hearing to be held under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

On appeal, the appellant submits the following arguments: 1. Did the RPD breach the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness with respect to interpretation, causing the appellant to experience an unfair hearing? 2. Is the RPD's credibility finding well-founded? 3. Did the RPD err in law in its analysis of the evidence on identity? DETERMINATION

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed. ANALYSIS Scope of the appeal
For questions of fact, of law, and of mixed fact and law, the RAD must apply the standard of correctness in accordance with Huruglica.2

I have conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence on the record, after listening carefully to the hearing, in order to form my own opinion about this refugee protection claim and to determine whether the decision rendered by the RPD is correct.
Having examined all of the testimonial and documentary evidence on the record, the RAD finds, as did the RPD, that the appellant failed to establish his identity and that he is not credible.
The very essence of this case is based on the appellant's credibility.

After listening to the recording of the hearing, which was nearly seven hours long, it is clear that the appellant's testimony was an arduous process. First, it should be noted that the appellant was unable to pinpoint when the major events of his life took place. For instance, he did not know when his life together with his spouse began, how old his children are, or when he resided in any given place. He was unable to specify when he pursued his studies, and yet his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) includes dates. The same can be said for his places of residence, which are included on the form. Moreover, it must be noted that the appellant did not respond directly to the questions he was asked. With a great deal of tact and patience, the member was required to restate and reformulate questions to finally obtain often random responses.

The first issue raised in the appellant's memorandum is that simultaneous interpreting errors breached principles of natural justice. First, it must be pointed out that the appellant's counsel understands the language spoken by the appellant. He has represented the appellant since the moment he arrived here. He has been the appellant's agent since he was placed in detention in Laval. He has accompanied and represented him throughout all proceedings, including those before the Immigration Division (ID), the RPD and now the RAD.

Before the ID, the appellant's counsel did not point out any interpretation errors. However, during the RPD hearings, he made a few remarks about words he considered to be incorrectly translated. Immediately, the member, who was attuned to the situation, stated [translation] "we are trying to help you, sir" when speaking of the dates of his common law life. She added that they will [translation] "help the gentleman pinpoint dates when there is a contradiction regarding a specific date of separation, we will reformulate the question...we are trying to help the gentleman situate himself in time because we have several responses about the same thing." When the appellant's counsel pointed out a few misunderstandings or an inadvertent misinterpretation, the member intervened to rectify the situation and reformulate the question, which was then interpreted without objection or response from the appellant's counsel; this tends to show that translation was adequate.3 Note that translation, based on the decision referenced, "does not require perfection," "the interpretation before the RPD must be adequate, continuous, precise, competent, impartial and contemporaneous."

On this issue, the RAD would like to state that the appellant's counsel never formally asked the member to stop the hearing and take steps to verify the translation in order to ensure that the work was adequate. If there were translation errors, it was his responsibility to point out the words and request that the hearing be stopped, which he failed to do. On a few occasions, he stated that a word was not translated correctly. The situation was addressed immediately by the presiding RPD member and the situation was clarified and rectified right away.

In his submissions at the end of the hearing, the appellant's counsel made a telling statement. The RAD wishes to emphasize it. He stated the following: [translation] "it must be stated, unassisted by the translator. I would not say that it affects the case, but I had to intervene because it did not seem to correspond to my client's statements."

The RAD is of the opinion that the statement by the appellant's counsel is telling. He has the opportunity to understand the language used by the appellant, he has a great deal of academic training, he is a good speaker, and the RAD can agree that on occasion, a word or string of words may not be translated in extenso because a word or image does not exist in the language used. Should, however, common sense and the response provided by the person not correspond to the question as asked, the member has a duty to confront the refugee protection claimant about the statement. In this case, the RAD is of the opinion that the hearing was conducted in an orderly fashion and went smoothly with two interpreters accredited by the IRB. Furthermore, the appellant's counsel was able to ensure that the translation was delivered by the book. Moreover, when the counsel raised issues, the member quickly addressed them and reworded the question to the appellant's benefit.

Given the circumstances, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant had a fair hearing that was lengthy, full and thorough, and that it did not violate section 14 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Therefore, the RPD hearings regarding the appellant's claim for refugee protection did not breach the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness.

The second topic put forward by the appellant is that the credibility finding is erroneous. The appellant adds that the RPD [translation] "fixated on the dates." For example, he did not know on what date he separated from his spouse, or how old the children were. The RAD wishes to state that it was not only regarding the dates that the appellant made errors.

For example, with respect to his place of residence, he interchanged the locations between his BOC Form and his testimony, not to mention the dates did not match up. His spouse's name is different in his testimony than in Exhibit D-4, the family composition certificate. This document, which was issued in November 2016-although at this time he was in Canada and had been here since XXXX XXXX, 2016-states that the couple are still together. His testimony indicates that they have been separated for quite some time.

Regarding his training, he testified that he is not highly educated. He indicated that he completed primary and secondary school but never finished his XXXX course. However, a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX issued on XXXX XXXX, 2005, namely, page 115 of the court record, is in evidence.

The panel could continue on with the appellant's passport. He indicated that it was his brother who took care of everything for his departure. Next, it was a certain Mr. XXXX who took over his case; then comes the version where it is the appellant who obtained the prized document for 400. It is the same thing for the photo used for the passport. The version changes throughout the hearing. Sometimes it was his brother who handled the photo, and then he stated that he accompanied Mr. XXXX to handle it, and finally, it was not the appellant who provided the photo. Regarding the photo, he testified that for the visa process he used one of eight copies developed. When confronted with the fact that the photo was found on his diploma issued 12 years earlier, he testified that it was possible there were some photos left. When asked to explain why the dates were inconsistent, the appellant was unable to provide a detailed and coherent explanation for it.

In providing these few examples, the RAD wishes to demonstrate that it is not only spotty testimony with regard to dates. It is true that he was unable to provide dates for the major past events in a person's life, such as their wedding, when children were born, a separation, even where they have lived. Despite all these forgotten dates, the rest of the appellant's testimony on sensitive topics was characterized by contradictions and inconsistencies, so much so that it cannot be given credit. The few examples referenced above obviously show that to be true.
Consequently, the RPD did not err with respect to the appellant's credibility.

The third and final topic raised regards the analysis of identity-related evidence. The RPD found that the appellant's credibility is completely undermined and that he failed to discharge his burden of proving his identity, pursuant to section 106 of the IRPA.

Regarding the certificate of nationality as opposed to citizenship, as indicated in the memorandum, the appellant stated that the RPD erred in limiting its analysis to factual issues surrounding this document. The appellant was vague with respect to how Exhibit D-1 was obtained. He stated that one day after he requested it, he picked up the document. It is clear that the document was issued on August 25, 2016, when the appellant was in Canada. This major contradiction, along with the other comments the appellant made about this exhibit, truly stand out. The RAD gives them no probative value.

Another document was analyzed by the panel. It is the voter's card. He stated that it is his first voter's card. He added that it was his first identification document and that his parents had suggested that he have this document made for travel purposes. The appellant's memorandum states that he obtained the voter's card according to the prevailing standards.

He testified that he lined up near a school, the authorities took his fingerprints and gave his name without further ado. The problem lies in his place of residence. He stated that he lives in his parents' home, but he also stated that he had not returned to his parents' home until 2016. In addition, the responses provided regarding the motivation for obtaining this card and where he resided lead the RAD to consider the path to obtaining the card unreliable.

The appellant states in paragraph 64 of his memorandum that [translation] "the panel gave no probative value to these documents because it believed they were fraudulent. How else can we explain its rejection of authentic documents out of hand?"

This unique case reveals an individual who filled in forms about his past with a great deal of information, and when it came time to present his past, he was incapable of providing a logical, accurate account free of inconsistencies. Perhaps this individual does not have a good memory, but how then did he provide so much detailed information to the various people he encountered over a period of months, such as his counsel, who was front and centre from the outset?

As it spent hours listening, the RAD notes that the appellant adjusts his testimony as the questions are asked of him. Explanations do not logically fit the questions, and sometimes they do not even match his earlier responses, which are contradicted as a result. He is incapable of providing coherent and plausible explanations about the passport photo he claims was taken in 2016 and is found on his diploma issued 12 years earlier. The places he has lived are another confusing matter. The places and locations change constantly throughout the testimony. The few items raised are highlighted to demonstrate that the evidence he submitted was not logically or even simply explained. On the contrary, the statements heard are a hodgepodge of contradictory facts that led the first panel to reject the claim for refugee protection based on a lack of identity. The RAD shares that analysis.
Consequently, the RAD finds that the RPD did not err.
For the reasons expressed in this decision, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD has rendered a correct and appropriate decision.

For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the same act.

The appeal is dismissed.
